proof:
# A density ratio of two does not preserve optimal sharp continuous depth

This is an exact obstruction to treating an arbitrary dominated density
addition as if it were log-concave. It does not refute the bounded-density
centroid inequality with factor gamma_d/2.

Let T be the standard triangle with barycentric coordinates
lambda_0=1-x-y, lambda_1=x, lambda_2=y. Let D=(1/10)T. The density

    f=1_T+1_D

is between one and two throughout the convex body T, and its total mass
is (101/100)|T|. Consider the three closed caps

    H_0={lambda_0>=169/500},
    H_1={lambda_1>=331/1000},
    H_2={lambda_2>=331/1000}.

Their thresholds sum to one, so the caps cover the entire plane: the
three barycentric coordinates always sum to one. D lies entirely in H_0
and is disjoint from H_1,H_2. Dividing masses by |T| gives

    integral_(H_0) f / |T|=(331/500)^2+1/100=112061/250000,
    integral_(H_1) f / |T|=integral_(H_2) f / |T|
                         =(669/1000)^2=447561/1000000.

The first of these is larger. Every candidate point therefore has a
containing closed cap with normalized mass at most

    112061/252500 < 4/9,

where the strict inequality is the integer calculation
4*252500-9*112061=1451>0. Thus even maximum halfspace depth can be below
gamma_2 for a density in [1,2] on a triangle. The example does not assert
that this law is an optimal target of any mixed-integer transport family.
